newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British manufacturers show signs of life.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British manufacturers show signs of life.

text.p: British manufacturers are showing signs of life, shrugging off the millstone of a strong pound, while the whole economy basks in the glow of low inflation, official data showed on Monday.
The Office for National Statistics said manufacturing output rose 0.6 percent in April, putting it 2.3 percent higher than it was a year ago. In March, output was up 1.2 percent year-on-year.

Pipeline inflation pressures remained almost completely absent. Prices leaving the factory gate -- output prices -- rose just 0.1 percent in May and were only one percent higher than this time last year.
"Domestic demand would seem to be more than offsetting any sterling-related weakness in export markets, helping manufacturing output to accelerate," said Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS.
April's robust 0.6 percent increase in output suggested the pound's 18 percent rally since last August was not hurting Britain's producers as much as had been thought.
The stronger sterling becomes, the more export prices rise and the harder manufacturers should find it to sell abroad.
Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko Europe, said a 0.5 percent annual increase in core output prices, excluding food, drink, tobacco and petrol, showed inflation was very subdued.
Raw materials prices paid by manufacturers, known as input prices, were 9.1 percent lower in April than a year ago.
"This should compensate for the stronger figures for industrial output," Briscoe said.
Overall industrial production, which measures manufacturing output together with energy production, jumped 1.2 percent in April.

But for most economists, it is the manufacturing sector -- the weak link in an otherwise buoyant British economy -- that is key. Any inflationary threat could come from a full-blown manufacturing recovery rather than dormant producer prices.

Cates said even though the inflation horizon remains unclouded for now, the latest batch of economic data lent weight to the decision to raise interest rates, taken by the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee at its first meeting on Friday.
The Bank, empowered by the new Labour government to set interest rates, raised base rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25.
"With today's data suggesting that manufacturing output is strengthening...sterling's strength would, at the moment, seem little cause for concern," Cates said.
Dharshini David of HSBC Markets agreed the recovery in manufacturing remained on track. But she said the adverse effects of the pound's rally were still feeding through.
"It would be premature to assume that manufacturing has escaped the effects of sterling's rise relatively lightly, as the worst is almost certainly yet to come," she said.
"Accordingly, the policy dilemma that has confronted the authorities over the last few months remains."

Britain's high streets are booming as consumer spending soars. The services sector, which accounts for two-thirds of gross domestic product (GDP), is showing healthy growth but manufacturing is much more sluggish.
As a result, many economists believe tax rises might be a more appropriate way of reining in the economy than interest rate rises, which could push the pound higher and hurt manufacturers even more.
All eyes are therefore on Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2.

"The conventional wisdom is that the best way to square the circle of strong domestic demand, but weak output, and strong sterling and pressure on interest rates, is some degree of fiscal restraint," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
"This would take some of the heat out of the retail sector and perhaps allow sterling to slip back."
